name: 16:8 time-restricted eating

lead: 16:8 time-restricted eating means eating all meals within eight hours and fasting for sixteen. It is popular for fat loss and a leaner look.
Trials are small and short, mostly in overweight adults and athletes, and reviews report weight loss broadly similar to ordinary calorie restriction.

paras: The window limits when food is eaten, which for many people reduces total calorie intake; researchers also study effects on fat oxidation and metabolic hormones.
Reported short-term effects include hunger, irritability, headaches and poor concentration. Reviews advise against it for pregnancy, youth, underweight people and those with eating disorders.

lead: 16:8 time-restricted eating (TRE) is a daily meal-timing pattern in which all food is eaten within an eight-hour window, leaving sixteen hours of fasting, often overnight plus part of the morning and evening. It belongs to the family of time-restricted eating, in which food is confined to a set daily window, commonly 8 to 12 hours.[1]

In looksmaxxing and wider fitness culture it is used mainly for leanness: people adopt it to reduce body fat, sharpen facial definition and simplify eating routines. Published trials have studied it in overweight adults, endurance athletes, cyclists, dancers and resistance-trained lifters, generally in small groups over weeks to months.[2][3][4][5]

Researchers describe the evidence on intermittent fasting as preliminary, with long-term effects not well studied, and reviews report that its advantage over ordinary calorie restriction is limited.[1]
infobox: Fat loss, metabolic markers, routine simplicity

paras: Time-restricted eating differs from alternate-day fasting and the 5:2 diet in that it does not change which days are fasted but limits the hours of each day in which food is eaten. The 16:8 version is the best-known variant. Stricter variants compress eating into one to two hours.[1]
Some versions align the window with daylight hours; others let the person choose a window that fits their schedule. A trial in middle-aged cyclists used a self-selected 16:8 window.[4][5]

Reviews of intermittent fasting generally report weight loss of roughly 2.5 to 9.9 percent in adults with overweight or obesity, mostly fat mass with some lean mass loss, and cardiometabolic changes broadly similar to those seen with continuous calorie restriction.[1]

Studies specific to 16:8 are small. In a seven-week trial, overweight adults following a low-calorie 16:8 pattern showed a trend toward weight loss, similar to that of a group following Orthodox religious fasting.[6]
Short-term effects reported for intermittent fasting include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired concentration, usually fading within about a month.[1]

Health authorities and reviews advise against these diets for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, underweight people and people with or prone to eating disorders; people with insulin-dependent diabetes are advised against them by some health ministries.[1]
An 8-week randomized trial in 23 male middle- and long-distance runners compared 16:8 TRE with habitual eating, measuring body composition, intake and endurance indices.[2]
A randomized trial in resistance-trained men and women tested hypercaloric 16:8 TRE alongside supervised resistance exercise, with both groups eating a 10 percent calorie surplus and high protein.[3]
Studies in middle-aged cyclists examined a self-selected 16:8 protocol on fat oxidation, cardiometabolic markers and 10-km cycling performance.[4][5]
A study of female DanceSport dancers examined body composition and lipolytic hormones under 16/8 TRE.[7]
Comparisons with Orthodox fasting examined anthropometric and metabolic profiles, plasma irisin and nesfatin-related outcomes in overweight adults.[6][8][9]

The pattern is discussed as a way to stay lean and reduce facial puffiness, often alongside calorie counting. Published studies of facial appearance under TRE were not located; reported outcomes concern body composition and metabolic markers.
